questions.question: What is the GIL in CPython?
questions.answer: The Global Interpreter Lock: only one thread at a time executes Python bytecode in a process.
questions.explanation: It keeps reference counting and the interpreter's internals simple and safe. Threads still help with I/O-bound work, because the lock is released while a thread waits on I/O. For CPU-bound work, use multiprocessing or native extensions. Python 3.13 added an optional free-threaded build that runs without the GIL.

questions.question: Why is a mutable default argument such as items=[] a trap?
questions.answer: The default is evaluated once, when the function is defined, so every call shares the same object.
questions.explanation: Appending to a default list changes it for all later calls that rely on the default. Use None as the default and create a new list inside the function.

questions.question: How does a generator differ from a function that returns a list?
questions.answer: It yields values one at a time and keeps its state between them, so the whole sequence never has to be in memory.
questions.explanation: Calling a generator function returns an iterator; each next() runs the body until the next yield. That suits large or endless sequences, and a pipeline of generators handles one item at a time from start to end.

questions.question: What is the difference between is and == in Python?
questions.answer: == compares values; is checks whether both names refer to the same object.
questions.explanation: == calls __eq__, so two separate lists with the same items are equal. Use is for identity checks against singletons such as None. CPython caches small integers and some strings, so is can seem to compare values, but that is an implementation detail you must not rely on.
